title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The past is made INSIDE the verb, not in front of it. meogeoyo becomes meogeosseoyo, jayo becomes jasseoyo, haeyo becomes haesseoyo. There is no word for 'did', no word for 'have', and nothing at all is added ahead of the verb — the whole change happens between the stem and the ending.

It is the same choice you already know, made twice. The stem vowel that picked -ayo or -eoyo in the present picks -asseoyo or -eosseoyo in the past, and a verb built on haeyo goes to haesseoyo. If you can conjugate the present you can conjugate the past.

There is ONE past. Korean does not divide it into 'I ate', 'I have eaten' and 'I did eat' — one form covers all three, and nothing in the sentence has to choose. If you have come from French or German, there is no auxiliary to pick here and nothing to agree with.

The copula has a past of its own, built the same way: haksaeng-ieyo becomes haksaeng-ieosseoyo, uisa-yeyo becomes uisa-yeosseoyo. It is still an ending on the noun, and it is still the last thing in the sentence.
eopseoyo has a past too: eopseosseoyo, 'there was not'. Absence is a verb in Korean, so it takes tense exactly as every other verb does — which is another reason it cannot be built out of a negative.
an does not move. It stays immediately in front of the verb in the past as in the present, and it still wedges into a verb made from a noun: gongbu an haesseoyo.

The time word does not do the work. Even with eoje sitting at the front of the sentence, the verb still has to carry the past — eoje bap-eul meogeoyo is not a past sentence, it is a broken one. That is the opposite of what the next module will show you about the future.

'Eat', and the past shape is the same word with the past piece pushed inside it: meogeosseoyo. Nothing has been added in front — no word for 'did', no word for 'have'.

sentences.trap: English builds a past with a helper — did, have — and Korean builds it with a piece INSIDE the verb. A learner reaching for a word to put in front of meogeoyo is reaching for something that has no seat in the sentence.
sentences.sound: UH-je BA-bul muh-GUH-ssuh-yo. The extra syllable in the middle is the past: muh-guh-SSUH-yo against the present's muh-GUH-yo. The ss is tense — pressed harder than an English s — and it is the sound that marks the tense.
